draft.title: Composition and inverse transformations
card: To do transformation A and then transformation B, multiply the matrices as BA. The matrix for the first transformation is written on the right, next to the point.
Order matters. BA is usually not the same as AB, so swapping the order can give a different result.
The inverse of a matrix M is written M⁻¹. It undoes M, so M⁻¹M is the identity matrix [1 0; 0 1], which leaves every point unchanged.
For [a b; c d], the inverse is 1/(ad − bc) × [d −b; −c a], when ad − bc is not 0. Example: the inverse of the dilation [2 0; 0 2] is 1/4 × [2 0; 0 2] = [1/2 0; 0 1/2], a dilation by 1/2.
draft.remember: Do A then B is BA. The inverse matrix undoes the transformation.

a.q: A is a reflection in the x-axis and B is a dilation by factor 3. Which matrix product does A first, then B?
a.why: The first transformation sits on the right, next to the point, so doing A then B is BA. AB would do B first, then A. Here the result happens to match, but the order of the product still needs to be right.
a.clue: The matrix closest to the point acts first.

b.q: M = [3 0; 0 5] stretches the plane. What is M⁻¹?
b.why: Here ad − bc = 15, so M⁻¹ = 1/15 × [5 0; 0 3] = [1/3 0; 0 1/5]. It undoes the stretch, so it scales x by 1/3 and y by 1/5. Swapping d and a without dividing by the 15 gives [5 0; 0 3], which is wrong.
b.clue: The inverse must undo the stretch of 3 in x and 5 in y.

problems.detail: A reflection in the x-axis and any dilation (by factor 3 from either axis, or uniform) are both diagonal matrices, so they commute and AB = BA. AB therefore also does A then B, and a careful student could defend it. The why even admits the results match. Choose transformations that do not commute (for example, a reflection and a rotation of 90°, or a shear) so that only BA is correct and the point that order matters is taught properly.
'A dilation by factor 3' does not say whether it is from the x-axis, from the y-axis or in both directions. VCE usually names the axis.

check.summary: Question a uses a reflection in the x-axis and a dilation, which commute, so AB gives the same result as BA and is also right. Swap in non-commuting transformations. Question b and the card are correct.

proposal.title: Composition and inverse transformations
card: To do transformation A and then transformation B, multiply the matrices as BA. The matrix for the first transformation is written on the right, next to the point.
Order matters. For A = [1 0; 0 −1] and B = [0 −1; 1 0], BA = [0 1; 1 0] but AB = [0 −1; −1 0]. Swapping the order can give a different result.
The inverse of a matrix M is written M⁻¹. It undoes M, so M⁻¹M is the identity matrix [1 0; 0 1], which leaves every point unchanged.

proposal.remember: Do A then B is BA. The inverse matrix undoes the transformation.

a.q: A = [1 0; 0 −1] reflects in the x-axis. B = [0 −1; 1 0] rotates 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Where does A then B send (1, 2)?
a.why: A then B is BA = [0 1; 1 0], which sends (1, 2) to (2, 1). Step by step, the reflection gives (1, −2) and the rotation then gives (2, 1). Doing B first, using AB, gives (−2, −1), which is the wrong order.
a.clue: The matrix closest to the point acts first.

b.q: M = [3 0; 0 5] stretches the plane. What is M⁻¹?
b.why: Here ad − bc = 15, so M⁻¹ = 1/15 × [5 0; 0 3] = [1/3 0; 0 1/5]. It undoes the stretch, so it scales x by 1/3 and y by 1/5. Swapping d and a without dividing by the 15 gives [5 0; 0 3], which is wrong.
b.clue: The inverse must undo the stretch of 3 in x and 5 in y.
